subcategory: Southwest desert native rock garden perennial

planting.note: Set out container transplants in spring into lean, gravelly, fast-draining soil in full sun; this subshrubby penstemon resents rich or regularly irrigated garden beds.

directions: Thurber's penstemon is a wiry, semi-woody subshrub of Chihuahuan and Sonoran desert grasslands and washes, with narrow aromatic gray-green leaves on slender branching stems. From spring into summer it sends up open spikes of small, pale pink to lavender tubular flowers that attract bees and hummingbirds despite their modest size. It thrives on neglect in lean, rocky or sandy soil with sharp drainage and needs almost no supplemental water once its roots are established. Hard shearing after the main bloom flush keeps the base from becoming woody and bare, and it pairs well with agave, cactus, and other low-water desert companions.

subcategory: Mojave Desert native rock garden perennial

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants into lean, rocky or sandy soil with sharp drainage in full sun; a thin gravel mulch helps prevent crown rot through wet winters.

directions: Native to rocky slopes and washes of the Mojave Desert's higher mountain ranges, this beardtongue forms a loose rosette of thick, waxy blue-green leaves from which rise slender stalks of bright rose-pink, flared tubular flowers in late spring. The glaucous foliage alone gives it strong textural value in a desert rock garden even before bloom. It needs sharp drainage and minimal summer water, and is best sited among boulders or on a slope where winter moisture drains away quickly. Deadheading spent stalks keeps the clump tidy and can prompt a secondary flush of bloom in favorable years.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

subcategory: Southern California chaparral native rock garden perennial

planting.note: Set out transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; it is adapted to summer-dry chaparral and declines quickly in heavy, regularly watered soil.

directions: Grinnell's beardtongue is a low, mound-forming perennial of the Transverse Ranges of Southern California, with soft gray-green, slightly woolly leaves and short spikes of pale lavender to pink flowers in late spring. Its compact habit makes it well suited to the front of a dry border or a sunny rock garden pocket, where it can be viewed up close. Like most chaparral penstemons it demands lean, sharply drained soil and goes dormant or declines under summer irrigation, so pair it with other true summer-dry natives. Trimming spent flower spikes after bloom keeps the mound neat for the rest of the season.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

subcategory: California Central Coast native pollinator perennial

planting.note: Set out container plants or direct sow with cold stratification in fall into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; avoid rich amended beds, which promote floppy growth.

directions: This mainland Central Coast variety of island buckwheat differs from the Channel Islands type by its deeper rose-red to brick-red flower heads, which age to rust tones and persist attractively through much of the season atop gray-green spoon-shaped foliage. It is a reliable bee and butterfly magnet and one of the longest-blooming of the native buckwheats in coastal and near-coastal gardens. Because it grows naturally on bluffs and coastal scrub, it wants lean soil, full sun, and sharp drainage, and tolerates salt spray and wind better than most garden perennials. Leave the dried flower heads standing into winter for seed-eating birds and added structure before cutting back.

planting.note: Set out small container plants or direct sow in fall into lean, rocky or gravelly soil with excellent drainage; this cushion-forming alpine buckwheat rots quickly in rich or poorly drained soil.

directions: Kennedy's buckwheat forms a tight, woody-based cushion of small, felted gray-green leaves that hugs rocky ground in the high mountains of Southern California and the southern Sierra Nevada. In summer it sends up short stalks topped with dense, rounded clusters of white to deep rose-pink flowers that age to rust, held just above the foliage mat. Its naturally alpine, scree-slope habitat makes it an excellent choice for a raised rock garden or trough planting with very sharp drainage and minimal organic matter in the soil. It needs almost no water once established and is best left undisturbed, since its cushion form resents transplanting once mature.
